topics.title: Proxy and Reflect
topics.summary: A Proxy intercepts operations on an object (get, set, delete...) and Reflect performs the default behaviour.
topics.description:
A **Proxy** wraps an object (the target) and lets you define **traps** that intercept fundamental operations. It is the basis of reactivity in Vue 3, validation layers, logging and mocking.

```js
const proxy = new Proxy(target, {
  get(target, prop, receiver) { return Reflect.get(target, prop, receiver); },
  set(target, prop, value, receiver) { return Reflect.set(target, prop, value, receiver); },
});
```

### Common traps
| Trap | Intercepts |
|---|---|
| `get` | reading a property |
| `set` | assigning a property |
| `has` | the `in` operator |
| `deleteProperty` | `delete obj.x` |
| `ownKeys` | `Object.keys`, `for...in` |
| `apply` | calling a function |
| `construct` | `new` on a function |

The `set` trap must return `true` for success (in strict mode returning `false` throws).

### Reflect
A built-in object whose methods mirror the proxy traps (`Reflect.get`, `set`, `has`, `ownKeys`, `apply`...). Use it inside traps to perform the **default operation** with correct `this` handling and a boolean result instead of exceptions.

### Use cases
- **Validation** - reject wrong types in `set`.
- **Default values** - return a fallback in `get` for missing keys.
- **Observable state** - run effects when data changes.
- **Logging / profiling** API calls.
- **Negative array indexes** or read-only views.

### Caveats
- Proxies add overhead; do not use them in hot loops.
- Private class fields (`#x`) do not work through a proxy.
- `proxy !== target`; identity checks can surprise.
keyPoints: Proxy wraps a target and intercepts operations via traps
Reflect provides the default behaviour inside traps
set trap must return true
Used for validation, reactivity, defaults and logging
Slower than direct access
pitfalls: Forgetting to return true from the set trap
Infinite recursion by touching the proxy inside its own trap
Private fields and built-ins like Map can break through proxies

examples.title: Validation and default values

interview.a: An object that wraps another object and intercepts operations like get, set and delete through handler traps, allowing custom behaviour.

interview.q: Why use Reflect inside proxy traps?
interview.a: Reflect methods perform the default operation with the correct receiver and return booleans, keeping the proxy behaving like the original.

interview.q: Name a framework that uses Proxy.
interview.a: Vue 3 uses Proxy for its reactivity system to track property reads and writes.

topics.title: Memory Management and Garbage Collection
topics.summary: JavaScript frees memory automatically when objects become unreachable; leaks happen when you keep references.
topics.description:
JavaScript manages memory for you. You create objects; the **garbage collector (GC)** frees them when they are no longer **reachable**.

### Life cycle
1. **Allocate** - creating objects, arrays, closures, strings.
2. **Use** - read and write.
3. **Release** - the GC frees unreachable memory.

### Reachability and mark-and-sweep
Starting from **roots** (global object, current stack, active closures), the GC **marks** everything reachable and **sweeps** (frees) the rest. Circular references are fine - if nothing reachable points to the cycle, it is collected. The old reference counting approach could not do this.

### Common memory leaks
1. **Accidental globals** (`leak = [];`).
2. **Forgotten timers**: `setInterval` callbacks keep their scope alive.
3. **Event listeners** never removed from DOM nodes that are discarded.
4. **Detached DOM nodes** still referenced from a variable or array.
5. **Closures** capturing large objects unnecessarily.
6. **Unbounded caches** (a `Map` that only grows).

### Prevent and detect
- Clear timers; remove listeners (or use `{ signal }` with AbortController).
- Use **WeakMap / WeakSet / WeakRef** for caches keyed by objects.
- Set references to `null` when finished with big data.
- Use browser DevTools: **Memory** tab, heap snapshots and the allocation timeline. A steadily rising line after repeated GC means a leak.

### Stack vs heap
Primitives and references live on the stack; objects live on the heap and are managed by the GC.
keyPoints: GC frees objects that are no longer reachable
Mark-and-sweep starts from roots
Leaks: globals, timers, listeners, detached DOM, large closures
Weak collections do not prevent collection
Use DevTools heap snapshots to find leaks
pitfalls: Assuming setting a variable to null always frees the memory immediately

examples.title: Cache with WeakMap vs Map

interview.q: How does garbage collection work in JavaScript?
interview.a: Engines use mark-and-sweep: they mark all objects reachable from roots (globals, stack) and free everything unmarked.

interview.q: Name common causes of memory leaks in JavaScript.
interview.a: Accidental globals, uncleared timers, undeleted event listeners, references to detached DOM nodes, closures holding large data and ever-growing caches.

interview.q: What is the benefit of WeakMap?
interview.a: Its keys are held weakly, so cached or associated data is automatically released when the key object is no longer referenced elsewhere.

topics.title: Debounce, Throttle and Memoization
topics.summary: Limit how often a function runs (debounce/throttle) or cache its results (memoize).
keyPoints: Debounce waits for a pause, then runs once
Throttle runs at most once per interval
Both are closures around a timer or flag
Memoize caches results of pure functions
Clear timers and limit cache size
pitfalls: Using debounce when you need regular updates (use throttle)
Losing this and arguments when wrapping functions

examples.title: Debounce, throttle and memoize
Live debounce and throttle counters
examples.html:
Type or move the mouse over the box:

move here
  • Raw events: 0
  • Debounced (400ms): 0
  • Throttled (400ms): 0

interview.a: Debounce delays execution until events stop for a given time and then runs once; throttle guarantees the function runs at most once in every interval during continuous events.

interview.q: When would you use debounce for search inputs?
interview.a: To avoid sending an API request on every keystroke - wait until the user pauses typing and then send a single request.
Caching the return value of a function for given arguments so repeated calls with the same input return the stored result instead of recomputing.

topics.title: Common Design Patterns
topics.summary: Reusable solutions: module, singleton, factory, observer (pub/sub) and more, expressed in JavaScript.
topics.description:
Design patterns are proven ways to structure code. JavaScript's closures, objects and modules make many of them very short.

### Module pattern
Use a closure (IIFE) or an ES module to hide private state and expose a small public API. In modern code every ES module file is a module.

### Singleton
Only **one instance** exists. An ES module that exports an object is naturally a singleton, because modules are evaluated once.
```js
export const config = Object.freeze({ api: "/v1" });
```

### Factory
A function that returns new objects, hiding the construction details: `createUser(type)`.

### Observer / Pub-Sub
Subjects keep a list of subscribers and notify them on change. DOM events and Node's `EventEmitter` are observers.
```js
const bus = {
  handlers: {},
  on(e, fn) { (this.handlers[e] ||= []).push(fn); },
  emit(e, data) { (this.handlers[e] || []).forEach((fn) => fn(data)); },
};
```

### Strategy
Swap algorithms at run time by passing functions (`sortBy(compareFn)`).

### Decorator / Higher-order wrapper
Add behaviour by wrapping a function: `withLogging(fn)`, `debounce(fn)`.

### Others worth knowing
- **Command** (undo/redo), **Iterator**, **Proxy**, **Mixin** (copy methods into classes), **Facade** (simple API over a complex one), **Dependency injection** (pass dependencies in).

### Advice
Do not force patterns. Start simple, and apply a pattern when the problem it solves appears.
keyPoints: Module hides state, exposes an API
Singleton: one shared instance (ES modules are naturally singletons)
Observer/pub-sub decouples emitters from listeners
Factory centralises object creation
Strategy and decorator use functions as values

examples.title: Event bus and factory

interview.a: A subject keeps a list of observers and notifies them automatically when its state changes. Examples are DOM events and EventEmitter.

interview.q: How do you create a singleton in JavaScript?
interview.a: Export a single instance from an ES module (modules run once and are cached), or use a closure that stores the instance.

interview.q: What is the module pattern used for?
interview.a: Encapsulating private variables and functions with a closure and exposing only a public interface.

topics.title: Performance Best Practices
topics.summary: Keep the main thread free, minimise DOM work and load only what you need.
topics.description:
Performance problems in JavaScript usually come from **blocking the main thread**, **too much DOM work** and **too much code**.

### Main thread
- Break long tasks into chunks (`setTimeout`, `requestIdleCallback`, `scheduler.yield()`).
- Move heavy computation to a **Web Worker** (`new Worker("worker.js")`, communicate with `postMessage`).
- Use `requestAnimationFrame` for animations instead of timers.
- Debounce and throttle high-frequency events; use `{ passive: true }` for scroll/touch listeners.

### DOM
- Batch reads and writes: reading `offsetHeight` after writing styles forces layout (**layout thrashing**).
- Use `DocumentFragment` or build HTML once instead of appending in a loop.
- Prefer `classList` toggles and CSS animations (`transform`, `opacity`).
- Use **event delegation** instead of many listeners.
- Virtualise very long lists.

### Code and data
- Choose the right data structure: `Set`/`Map` for lookups instead of `array.includes` in loops.
- Avoid nested loops over large arrays (O(n^2)).
- Do not create functions or objects inside hot loops unnecessarily.
- Memoize expensive pure functions.

### Loading
- **Code splitting** with dynamic `import()`.
- `defer` / `async` on scripts, lazy-load images and below-the-fold content (IntersectionObserver).
- Minify and compress (gzip/brotli), cache with HTTP headers.

### Measure first
Use DevTools Performance and Lighthouse; `performance.now()` and `console.time()` for quick tests. Optimise measured bottlenecks, not guesses.
keyPoints: Never block the main thread with long synchronous work
Batch DOM changes and avoid layout thrashing
Pick efficient data structures (Map/Set)
Split code and lazy load resources
Measure with DevTools before optimising
pitfalls: Interleaving DOM reads and writes in loops

examples.title: Measuring array search vs Set

interview.q: What is layout thrashing and how do you avoid it?
interview.a: Alternating DOM reads (that force layout) and writes causes repeated reflows. Batch all reads first, then all writes, or use requestAnimationFrame.

interview.q: How can you run heavy computation without freezing the UI?
interview.a: Move it to a Web Worker, or split it into small chunks scheduled with setTimeout/requestIdleCallback.

interview.q: Why use a Set instead of an array for lookups?
interview.a: Set.has is on average O(1) while Array.includes is O(n), which matters inside loops.

topics.title: Security Basics: XSS and Safe Coding
topics.summary: Never insert untrusted data as HTML, avoid eval, and keep secrets out of client code.
topics.description: Front-end security is about not letting attacker-controlled data become **executable code** in your page. ### Cross-site scripting (XSS) XSS happens when untrusted input (a comment, a URL parameter, an API field) is inserted into the page as HTML and a script runs with your site's privileges - it can read `localStorage`, cookies, make requests as the user, or rewrite the page. ```js // DANGEROUS div.innerHTML = userComment; // // SAFE div.textContent = userComment; ``` ### Safe practices - Use **`textContent`** or `setAttribute` for text; avoid `innerHTML`, `outerHTML`, `insertAdjacentHTML`, `document.write` with user data. - If you must render HTML, sanitise with a library like **DOMPurify**. - Never use `eval()`, `new Function(string)` or `setTimeout("string")`. - Validate URLs: block `javascript:` links before setting `href`. - Frameworks (React, Vue) escape output by default; avoid `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` / `v-html` with untrusted data. ### Other essentials - **Content Security Policy (CSP)** header limits where scripts can load from. - Keep **tokens in HttpOnly cookies**, not in localStorage. - **CSRF**: use SameSite cookies and CSRF tokens for state-changing requests. - **Never put secrets** (API keys, passwords) in front-end code - everyone can read it. - Validate and sanitise on the **server** as well; client checks are only for UX. - Keep dependencies updated (`npm audit`). - Use `rel="noopener noreferrer"` on `target="_blank"` links. ### Remember Treat **all** input as untrusted: user text, URL, cookies, postMessage, third-party APIs.
keyPoints: XSS = untrusted input executed as script
Use textContent instead of innerHTML for user data
Sanitise HTML with DOMPurify when HTML is required
Never use eval or build code from strings
Secrets do not belong in front-end code
pitfalls: Assuming data from your own API is always safe
Using innerHTML for convenience with template strings

examples.title: Escaping untrusted HTML

interview.q: What is XSS and how do you prevent it?
interview.a: Cross-site scripting is injecting malicious script into a page through untrusted data. Prevent it by escaping or using textContent, sanitising any HTML, using CSP and avoiding eval and innerHTML with user input.

interview.q: Why is it risky to store JWT tokens in localStorage?
interview.a: Any XSS script can read localStorage and steal the token. HttpOnly cookies cannot be read by JavaScript.
No. It improves user experience but can be bypassed, so the server must validate and sanitise every request.
